newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Concern Belgrade stresses survival over economy.
newsitem.headline: Concern Belgrade stresses survival over economy.

text.p: Yugoslavia has entered 1997 with a sudden slide in the dinar currency, raising concern that the embattled Socialist government might neglect the economy to save itself, economists said on Wednesday.
The dinar's real commercial rate, set on the streets, was 3.8 to the German mark at the end of 1996. After eight days of Christmas/New Year holidays, it has sunk as low as 4.3.
In the meantime, the official rate remains fixed at 3.3.
Economists said the dinar's losses resulted from an alarming monetary expansion during the last 10 days of December.
"The central bank gave in to Serbian government pressures to print money and cover its fiscal deficit," Pavle Petrovic of the CES-Mecon private economic research institute said.

Money supply data, in the safe keeping of the central bank, is impossible to obtain. But unofficial estimates put the country's growth in M1 money supply at at least 10 percent, or 500 million dinars ($97 million), towards the end of December.
That much money alone was needed in Serbia to pay pension arrears, economists said.

Opposition parties, who have protested in the streets for seven weeks over election fraud by the Socialists, accuse Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's government of printing money to pay back wages to the police.

"It is evident that social and political stability are threatened (by weeks of opposition protests) and that the government is trying to save whatever remains to be saved at the expense of the economy," one economist said.

"For a long time, our governments could not stand up to the economic and political situation the country was in. They all give in to the very first serious temptation," said the economist, who asked not to be named.
"And right now Yugoslavia is experiencing rapid deterioration both internally and externally.

"The situation resembles 1993, when the economy was in the hands of so-called "successful businessmen'. It is a deadly situation to have (government) ministers and businessmen in one person. The economy must be run by sober minds," the economist said.
Economists said the government would have to recognise the big change in the dinar rate through an official devaluation of the currency but it was difficult to say when this would happen.
"Devaluation is a political decision and the dinar will devalue on political will only," an economist said.

Analysts said the protest wave itself had not damaged the economy because production was only half what it was in 1991, the year federal Yugoslavia broke up in war that lasted four years. Unofficial unemployment exceeds 50 percent.
"All this protest can only bring us true democracy, faster reforms and an open market economy," one economist said.
Analysts said the dinar's problems resulted from government pressure on the central bank to resort to printing presses to cover its growing fiscal deficits.
Petrovic said the government had lost credibility built up since 1994, when it promised it would "never ever again resort to central bank funds to cover its fiscal imbalance".
"The damage is immense, credibility lost, the dinar stability ruined, but the government must do something to put an end to this misfortune," he added.
Petrovic called on the government to adopt a mini-economic package to restore monetary stability and warned that inaction would lead to hyperinflation, as was seen in 1993.
Such a package should aim at a radical reduction of the money supply and the central bank must intervene on the official interbank foreign exchange market to calm the dinar.
The government should also consider freezing wages for several months, Petrovic added.

"Nothing in an economy happens accidentally. If we ended 1996 with December-on-December inflation of 60 percent, while the dinar rate remained artificially stable, the correction in the dinar black market rate was inevitable," said Danilo Sukovic of the Institute of Social Science.
